CTO Interview with Paweł Banachowicz of Silicon Creationsby Daniel Nenni on 11-17-2026 at 12:00 pm

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: Chiplet, FinFET, GAA, IP, Silicon Creations

Key takeaways ▼

Paweł Banachowicz is a Director of Analog & Mixed-Signal Design at Silicon Creations, where he has worked since 2012. He has designed or led the design of hundreds of PLL and clocking IPs, with a focus on FinFET and GAA processes, and played a key role in building the company’s advanced-node design infrastructure from 16nm onward. He was the lead designer of Silicon Creations’ first FinFET product in 2013. Silicon Creations’ IP is now in production in over 2,000 chips.
What brought you to Silicon Creation?
It was June 2012. I was in the second semester of my master’s program at the University in Krakow, spending evenings in the lab on hobby projects in analog IC design and layout. My plan was to join Silicon Valley forces one day and work on chip design. I had even discussed a job abroad after graduation.
During one of those sessions, an unexpected guest told us he had opened an office nearby and they were just a couple of guys in the US and Poland looking for engineers to design PLLs and SerDes in 28nm – state of the art back then – with only a handful of companies having access. We met again, on a Skype call, and I started the following month as employee number eight. That guest was Michal Bombar, Silicon Creations Krakow site manager; on the call were co-founders Randy Caplan and Jeff Galloway.
Soon I was tasked with designing our flagship PLL in TSMC’s 16nm process, using a super-early PDK for the first MPW in that node. It prepared us for the FinFET revolution and became a turning point. The rest is history: almost 200 employees, more than 500 unique PLL products, over 2,000 chips taped out with our IP at TSMC, 2nm in high volume mass production and sub-2nm test chips taped out by our customers using our solution with more to come.
What is the biggest challenge your customer is facing?
I think the biggest challenge is that chip design cycles have shrunk and everything has accelerated. In the past, five years from product idea to mass production was typical. Mobile SoCs led in new nodes; HPC CPUs and GPUs followed two or three years later. Automotive, industrial and aerospace came even later. Along the way, teams made multiple test chips to prove building locks, systems and prototypes before manufacturing.
Now all markets compete at or near bleeding-edge processes, without waiting for maturity. Chiplets mitigate yield issues in large monolithic designs, and companies often make only one test chip before going to production. AI computational demand across mobile, automotive, HPC and even IoT is driving this. To survive, you need the best PPA available in the latest nodes.
The cost of failure was always high, but now it is on an unimaginable level. To meet aggressive schedules and market expectations, you need solid, low-risk, predictable foundations. That’s what we at Silicon Creations provide: analog and mixed-signal building blocks that just work.
Why is your approach to solving this problem unique?
Think of Silicon Creations as an extension of your internal team. The IP tarball you receive is not just GDS geometries for manufacturing masks; it also represents 20 years of experience across chip designs, processes and major foundries. Our engineers work with your team on clocking and I/O architecture, IP selection, integration and new solutions. When we ask customers what makes us unique, the most common answer is quick, direct support.
Our motto is “We’re successful when you are.” We want customers to experience that through honest, prompt answers even when a pre-sale technical meeting ends with a shorter IP purchase list and a more robust, elegant solution. The last thing we want is years of silicon debug and money spent on masks because we overpromised. Semiconductor IP is not just about performance; it is about de-risking chips and preparing for what large-scale manufacturing can throw at you.
What other approaches are being used to solve this problem?
Reliable technology that works at scale in real-world applications is our baseline. Younger engineers sometimes point to much better performance in a scientific paper or conference. No doubt you can achieve enormous gains when designing five chips in typical silicon for a narrow application, at room temperature with a pristine laboratory power supply. But the Figure of Merit being optimized may no longer have practical meaning. Take integrated phase jitter from 12kHz to 20MHz, defined for SONET networks and still used to compare PLLs. Our friends at SiTime have written about this:
A Modern Approach to Refclk Jitter Analysis for SerDes Applications
We aim for something different: a wide range of industry parameters; flexibility to reuse IP across applications and reduce customer time and cost; extensive testability and debug features; and resilience when switching digital circuits make supplies far from ideal. We verify at extreme PVT conditions, including mismatch and lifetime device degradation. There is also some secret sauce: being conservative about effects not modeled but known from years of silicon experience.
We grow the team organically, emphasizing quality, simplicity and attention to detail. We push the envelope, but in a safe and predictable way.
What challenges will your customers face in the near future?
I read this as what we are working on today to mitigate challenges customers will face when their products reach the market. We are doing a lot with DVFS, Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling. It is about staying in the PPA sweet spot as conditions change. Chips need to run at the limit, wake computing units quickly for heavy workloads, adjust to temperature, power density and supply dips, and sleep whenever possible to conserve energy. Performance per watt drives the industry.
We have prepared sensing and actuation solutions that detect slow and fast voltage movements, temperature, latency and device degradation, then regulate the clock to maintain optimum performance and mitigate large supply dips or thermal runaway.
We have especially exciting developments in fast clock changes: a line of IPs that can change clock frequency from pretty much any frequency to another in under a nanosecond, without multiple clock sources.
How has AI changed your business strategy?
AI accelerated everything. Existing customers launched new projects, while customers that didn’t exist yesterday suddenly began developing dozens of AI chips in parallel. We needed to scale delivery quickly without unhealthy expansion or compromising quality.
We have always written internal software, scripts and tools for our specialized IC engineering work. AI now helps engineers build more complex data-analysis instruments, shorten design cycles and deepen understanding of our IP. Our internal knowledge database—manuals, training, articles and years of experience is connected to agentic AI running on our servers and accessible to employees.
But not everything is that beautiful. There are risks. Foundries have forbidden feeding PDK-related data to AI, including on-premises agents. We cannot train LLMs on customer data, either. Human in the Loop remains critical, so we have implemented protections and trained our people. Customers still speak with real engineers, now empowered by 20 years of accumulated knowledge—not chatbots giving copy-pasted manual answers. They get direct access to senior architects.
Forget about handing DRM and SPICE models to an agent and asking it to design a chip. That may happen on LinkedIn with open academic PDKs, but real work has constraints. Generic tasks and open SPICE models do offer room for AI optimization. Digital teams have even more freedom because HDL is technology agnostic. Engineers can integrate controllers such as DisplayPort, Ethernet and PCIe, create FPGA glue logic, write firmware and generate test patterns and eye-scan results in days rather than months. It works—but you still need an engineer who knows what to ask, what results to expect and how to catch fundamental mistakes.
